patterns.usage_note: A sentence-final particle of Kansai and other western dialects, tacked onto plain forms to push back at the listener: the speaker is irritated that the hearer has missed something obvious or is making him repeat himself. It is spoken language and appears in writing mainly as dialogue; standard-Japanese equivalents are 〜じゃないか and 〜だろ. After a noun or na-adjective it rides on the Kansai copula や, so the shape is 〜やがな rather than 〜だがな. Do not confuse it with the archaic optative 〜もがな, which is a separate construction.

examples.ruby: それくらいのこと、自分[じぶん]でできるがな。
examples.english: Come on, you can manage that much yourself.

examples.ruby: 昨日[きのう]のうちにちゃんと電話[でんわ]したがな。
examples.english: I called you yesterday, I told you.

examples.ruby: この荷物[にもつ]、一人[ひとり]で運[はこ]ぶには重[おも]いがな。
examples.english: Come on, this thing is way too heavy to carry alone.

patterns.usage_note: Takes a bare noun, typically a person or thing in the speaker's own orbit, and sets it up as a topic the speaker is about to complain about; the following clause is almost always a negative evaluation. It is far more emotive than plain は or 〜については. The pattern has no polite variant: it stays 〜ときたら even in otherwise polite speech, because the complaint itself is a lapse into familiarity. Where がな vents at the listener, ときたら vents about someone or something not present.

examples.ruby: うちの部長[ぶちょう]ときたら、人[ひと]の話[はなし]を全然[ぜんぜん]聞[き]かない。
examples.english: Honestly, my department head never listens to a word anyone says.

examples.ruby: 最近[さいきん]の天気[てんき]ときたら、朝[あさ]と夜[よる]で別世界[べっせかい]だ。
examples.english: The weather lately is absurd; morning and night feel like different worlds.

examples.ruby: あの店[みせ]の接客[せっきゃく]ときたら、思[おも]い出[だ]すだけで腹[はら]が立[た]つ。
examples.english: The service at that place, ugh, just remembering it makes my blood boil.
